Hi Alan,

Thanks — good questions. Short answers up front, longer detail below:

1) Transit vs processed PHI: If the request body contains identifiable patient data and it is sent to Redwood's hosted inference endpoints, Redwood would treat that as PHI in scope for a BAA.
2) Minimum architecture to avoid PHI retention: Use Redwood Dedicated or Private deployment so customers control the network boundary and key management. On hosted API, we can support no-persist logging and strict max-retention, but hosted endpoints still process the data and would therefore fall under BAA scope.
3) De-id + fallback: If de-identification is performed client-side and you only ever send tokenized payloads, that materially reduces PHI scope. However, the fallback path where raw identifiers could be sent means you should assume PHI transit and request a BAA unless you can guarantee the fallback is disabled or blocked before it reaches Redwood.

Recommended next steps:
- For a pilot: consider Redwood Dedicated with restricted ingress (IP allowlist) + KMS integration so you can rotate keys. That gives the clearest contractual posture.
- If you must use hosted for rapid onboarding: we'll need BAA language and an operational runbook showing how you prevent fallback transmissions; we'll also provide SOC 2 Type II evidence and a data retention attestation.

I'll loop in Dev and Laura below to confirm technical controls and whether we can provide a configuration checklist you can attach to the SOW.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Head of Trust & Security (Acting)
Redwood Inference

Soojin / Laura,

Quick notes on implementation constraints:
- Hosted API: TLS terminates at our gateway; we do not currently offer end-to-end customer-managed TLS for hosted endpoints (that is available on Private/Dedicated via peering). So any raw PHI sent to hosted endpoints is technically accessible within our control plane for routing (we can and do disable persistent logs on a per-customer basis and purge KV caches, but that does not remove the processing appetite).
- Dedicated: Runs in isolated GPU pools, supports VPC peering + customer KMS (bring-your-own-key) for session-level encryption. We can provide a retention policy window (e.g., 24h ingest logs) and attestation for a pilot.
- De-id flow: We can help validate that tokenization is irreversible; recommend a short HMAC with key you manage for mapping tokens back on your side. If fallback paths exist, we should add a network-layer reject (403) if payloads match a PHI pattern.

I'll draft a short technical checklist (network + KMS + logging + response headers) for Soojin to share. Also flagging that SOC 2 and our standard BAA template are available; legal will add the specific clause about transit/processing.

-Dev

Hi Alan — following up with the checklist and next steps.

Summary of agreed position for pilot:
- Because the fallback path could surface raw identifiers, Redwood will require a BAA for the pilot if you continue to use hosted API endpoints.
- We recommend Redwood Dedicated for production access to avoid ambiguity; Dedicated allows VPC peering, customer-managed KMS, and stricter ingress controls which materially reduce Redwood-side access to raw payloads.
- If you can guarantee that the fallback path is blocked or returns an on-client error (i.e., never transmits identifiers to Redwood), you may proceed without a BAA but we will still need the dataflow attestation and a short runbook as part of onboarding.

Requested items from CareProxy to proceed:
1) Which deployment do you prefer for the pilot (hosted vs dedicated)?
2) Signed NDA + requested BAA (we can send our standard BAA and SOC 2 evidence)
3) Network diagram if you change the dataflow after de-id — we'll re-review for residual risk.

I attached a short technical checklist and our BAA template for convenience. If you'd like, we can set a 30-minute call to get legal / security teams aligned.

Best,
